blocks.text: Chapter 8.
Relaxation and Randomness: Solving the Unsolvable
Eighth night, friend — and it begins with a young lawyer on horseback, crossing the Illinois prairie of the 1840s.

Twice a year he rides the circuit — a loop of county courthouses, town after town, hundreds of muddy miles — and he'd dearly love the shortest route that visits every town once and brings him home. The lawyer's name is Abraham Lincoln. And the puzzle he's living has a modern name — the traveling salesman problem — and a terrible secret: it explodes. Routes multiply factorially, and decades of research say no algorithm can guarantee the best tour without essentially trying them all. Computer science calls such problems intractable — and here's tonight's twist, friend: they're everywhere in your life. Seating charts. Schedules. Itineraries. Provably, officially too hard for perfection.

And that, strangely, is liberating. Because when perfection is mathematically out of reach, agonizing over it isn't diligence — it's a category error. Tonight: how the professionals actually solve the unsolvable — by cheating beautifully, and by rolling dice on purpose.
Relax the problem

The first family of tricks is relaxation: deliberately solve an easier version of your problem, then translate back. Remove a constraint: drop the salesman's visit-once-in-a-loop rule and you get the minimum spanning tree — the cheapest network connecting all towns, computable in a blink — whose cost bounds the best possible tour, and tracing around it yields a real tour guaranteed at most twice optimal (in practice, within a few percent). Allow fractions: the NP-hard party-invitation problem — smallest set of invitees so everyone you care about knows someone coming — becomes easy if you can invite someone half-way; solve the fractional version, then round up, with a proof you're within a factor of two. And subtlest of all, turn rules into prices — Lagrangian relaxation: "impossible" becomes "expensive." The man who schedules Major League Baseball lives by it, because satisfying every stadium, broadcaster, and league rule at once is literally infeasible — so some constraints must become penalties you can choose to pay. Hear the life translation, friend: when your to-do list is infeasible, the answer isn't paralysis. It's deciding which "musts" are actually prices.
Roll the dice

Pause and guess: 1946. Mathematician Stanislaw Ulam, recovering from illness, is playing solitaire — and wondering about the odds of winning a hand. The combinatorics are hopeless: too many possibilities to compute. Then he has an idea that would end up powering nuclear physics at Los Alamos. What was it?
Ready? Here is what happened.

Just deal the hands and count. Stop deriving — sample. Deal a hundred random hands, see how many win, and you have an estimate no analysis could deliver. With John von Neumann he forged this into the Monte Carlo method — when a system has too many interacting possibilities to enumerate, simulate random instances — and it became indispensable to the bomb physicists and then to every field that models complexity. And randomness delivers guarantees, too, friend: modern cryptography needs enormous primes, and the Miller-Rabin test certifies them by randomized challenge — each round, a composite number has at most a 1-in-4 chance of slipping through, so a few dozen rounds push the error below one in a septillion — less likely than a hardware glitch. Every secure web connection you've ever opened rests on primes certified only almost certainly. The Bloom filter plays the same trade for memory: a data structure that answers "have I seen this before?" in a fraction of the space, with rare false positives and zero false negatives — how search engines avoid re-crawling the web. The pattern, friend: tolerate a small, tunable error, and impossible scales become routine.
The trap of the local peak

Many hard problems yield to a humble strategy: start with any solution, make small improvements, repeat — hill climbing. Swap two cities in the tour; keep the swap if it's shorter. The fatal flaw: the local maximum — a solution no small change can improve... which may still be far from the best. The landscape of solutions is rugged, friend, full of minor peaks that trap pure improvers. And take the human parallel seriously: if your routine, career, or portfolio is merely un-improvable by any small tweak — that certifies only a local peak. The escapes, in rising elegance: jitter — when stuck, make a few random changes even if they hurt, then climb again; random restarts — scrap everything, begin somewhere random, keep the best peak found; and the Metropolis algorithm — always accept improvements, and sometimes accept bad moves, with probability shrinking the worse the move is.

Pause and guess: In the early 1980s, IBM physicists Kirkpatrick and Gelatt faced chip layout — an NP-hard nightmare ruled by expert human intuition. Being physicists, they borrowed a trick from METALLURGY. What was it — and what happened to the human experts?
Ready? Here is what happened.

Annealing. A blacksmith gets strong, flawless metal not by cooling it fast — that locks in defects — but by heating it and cooling it slowly, letting the atoms explore before they settle. So they gave the Metropolis algorithm a temperature: run the search hot at first, accepting even large steps backward... then cool it gradually until it becomes a strict hill climber accepting only improvements. Simulated annealing, published in Science in 1983 — and it promptly beat IBM's expert human chip designers, going on to become one of the most practical tools ever found for NP-hard problems, from circuits to airline schedules. Its deepest lesson is about ordering, friend: randomness belongs at the beginning; rigor belongs at the end. Front-load your wildest experimentation when commitments are few — new job, new project, new city — and become progressively harder to dislodge as the design matures. The artists found the same law independently: Brian Eno's Oblique Strategies deck — cryptic cards drawn at random ("Honor thy error as a hidden intention") to jolt stuck studio sessions. The random card works because it's irrelevant: it samples the solution space at a distance no incremental thinking reaches. When truly stuck, friend, don't push harder uphill. Add heat.
Before you go

So: Lincoln's circuit was provably intractable, and perfection there is a category error; relax the problem — drop a constraint, allow fractions, turn musts into prices — and carry a guarantee back; Ulam dealt the hands instead of computing them, and the web's security rests on almost-certain primes; small improvements strand you on local peaks; and the annealer's schedule — wild early, strict late — beat the experts and governs careers as well as silicon. This week, friend: find one thing in your life that's "un-improvable by small tweaks"... and inject one random change you'd normally reject.

One night remains in this book — and it saves the biggest question for last: what happens when everyone else is optimizing too? Tomorrow: the poker table where thinking harder makes you worse; why traffic jams and packed parties are mathematically inevitable; the auction where every bidder is rational and everyone loses — and the book's final, gentle commandment: computational kindness. Next time, the finale: living among other optimizers.
Key takeaways
Some problems are provably intractable — for NP-hard puzzles like the traveling salesman, demanding perfection is a category error.
Relaxation: solve the easier version — drop a constraint (spanning tree), allow fractions then round, or price the impossible (Lagrangian) — with quality guarantees.
Monte Carlo: when analysis is hopeless, sample — deal the hands and count.
Miller-Rabin and Bloom filters: accept a tiny, tunable error rate and impossible scales become routine.
Hill climbing strands you on local maxima — escape with jitter, random restarts, or Metropolis's occasional accepted bad move.
Simulated annealing beat the chip experts: run hot early, cool slowly — schedule your randomness at the start, your rigor at the end.
